Each guide should include real-world disclosed examples (redacted) and practice scenarios.

sprints.title: The Hunting Grounds — API security testing methodology

GraphQL testing: introspection queries, batching attacks, nested query DoS, authorization bypass via field-level access, mutation abuse. gRPC testing: reflection abuse, message tampering. API documentation analysis: Swagger/OpenAPI spec mining, Postman collection extraction, undocumented endpoint discovery. Tools: Burp Suite with API-specific extensions, Postman, Insomnia, mitmproxy, OWASP ZAP API scan, kiterunner for API endpoint brute-forcing. Include OWASP API Security Top 10 mapped to hunting techniques.

Azure: blob storage enumeration, Azure AD tenant discovery, exposed App Services, Key Vault access misconfigs, Azure Functions auth bypass. GCP: public Cloud Storage buckets, Firebase database exposure (common in mobile apps), GCP metadata server, Cloud Functions auth issues. Multi-cloud: Kubernetes misconfigs (exposed dashboards, etcd, kubelet), Docker registry exposure, Terraform state file leaks, CI/CD pipeline secrets. Tools: ScoutSuite, Prowler, CloudMapper, Pacu, enumerate-iam, cloud_enum. Protocol-level: DNS zone transfer, DNS rebinding, BGP hijacking concepts, SSL/TLS misconfigs (testssl.sh, sslyze — expired certs, weak ciphers, HSTS absence), mail server misconfigs (open relays, SPF/DKIM/DMARC failures, email spoofing). Infrastructure: VPN misconfigs, exposed admin panels (Shodan queries), printer/IoT device exposure, IPMI/BMC access, exposed database ports (MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Memcached). Wireless: rogue AP detection, WPA2 enterprise misconfigs. sprints.title: The Hunting Grounds — Cryptographic vulnerability hunting

Session management: predictable session tokens, session fixation, cookie security flags (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite). Encryption flaws: padding oracle attacks, ECB mode detection (penguin problem), weak key generation, hardcoded encryption keys, IV reuse. Certificate issues: self-signed certs in production, expired certificates, wildcard cert abuse, certificate transparency monitoring. Password storage: identifying weak hashing (MD5, SHA1 without salt), timing attacks on comparisons. Randomness: weak PRNG detection, predictable tokens/codes (password reset, email verification, API keys). Cross-references key house cryptography curriculum for foundational knowledge.

sprints.title: The Hunting Grounds — Source code review and static analysis

SAST tools: Semgrep (custom rules), CodeQL (GitHub), SonarQube, Bandit (Python), Brakeman (Ruby), SpotBugs (Java), ESLint security plugins. Open-source audit: finding bugs in OSS dependencies (npm audit, Snyk, dependency confusion), reviewing recent commits for security-relevant changes, GitHub Advanced Security features. sprints.title: DNS Resolver Race — Racing Game
sprints.notes: Racing game where players compete against the clock to resolve DNS queries through the full resolution chain. CONCEPT: Player races a DNS query through the resolution hierarchy — client cache, recursive resolver, root nameserver, TLD nameserver, authoritative nameserver — choosing the correct path at each hop. Wrong hops = time penalties or dead ends. Cache hits act as speed boosts / shortcuts. GAMEPLAY IDEAS (TBD — design not finalized): (1) Side-scroller runner where the query packet is the character, lanes represent different nameserver choices, and correct hops accelerate while wrong ones slow/redirect. (2) Point-and-click path chooser: visual network map, click the correct next-hop server to advance. Timer runs throughout — faster completion = higher score. (3) Could incorporate record types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, PTR) as different challenge modes. (4) TTL mechanic — cached records expire, forcing re-resolution through the full chain. sprints.title: Anti-Cheat Rule — Quiz Integrity Enforcement
sprints.notes: ANTI-CHEAT RULE: Three mandatory requirements for ALL quizzes platform-wide. (1) NO IMMEDIATE FEEDBACK — feedback, correct/incorrect indicators, and explanations must ONLY appear after the entire quiz is submitted. No green/red per question. No explanation popups mid-quiz. Review screen with explanations appears post-submission only. (2) ANSWER ROTATION — answer option positions must be randomized (Fisher-Yates shuffle) on every quiz load. Student sees A/B/C/D in different order each attempt. Correct answer index must be remapped after shuffle. (3) QUESTION POOLING — quizzes should draw from a larger question bank than displayed. Minimum: 50% more questions than shown (e.g., bank of 15, show 10). Question selection AND order randomized per attempt. AUDIT FINDINGS (228 files): 157 standalone quiz files (69%) have ALL three violations — immediate per-question feedback with green/red styling, fixed answer positions hardcoded in arrays, and identical question sets every attempt. Only 32 quizzes (~14%) use shared engines with any protections (QuizEngine.js has optional randomize/showFeedback; WSA quiz-engine.js has exam-mode with deferred feedback). 10 Cloud CSE quizzes cache full answer data in localStorage (DevTools inspectable). IMPLEMENTATION STRATEGY: Phase 1 — Update shared engines: (a) QuizEngine.js — set showFeedback:false as DEFAULT (not opt-in), ensure randomize:true is enforced not optional. Add question pool/draw mechanics. (b) WSA quiz-engine.js — already compliant on feedback deferral, add question pooling. Phase 2 — Migrate standalone quizzes: Convert the 157 standalone .quiz.html files to use QuizEngine.js with anti-cheat defaults. This is the bulk of the work. Group by house for systematic conversion: cloud (48 quizzes), forge/comptia (42 quizzes), eye/cysa (28 quizzes), shield (15 quizzes), script/linux (12 quizzes), web (8 quizzes), key (4 quizzes). Phase 3 — Question bank expansion: For each converted quiz, expand question arrays from current 10 to 15+ questions. Draw 10 per attempt. Prioritize high-traffic quizzes first (core certification tracks: A+, Security+, CySA+, Cloud+). Phase 4 — Storage cleanup: Remove localStorage caching of full answer arrays in Cloud CSE quizzes. Store only pass/fail status and score, never individual answers or correct answer keys. MARATHON SUITABILITY: Phase 1-2 are highly marathonable — systematic find-and-replace pattern across 157 files with clear before/after requirements. Phase 3 (question bank expansion) requires subject matter knowledge to write new questions. FILES: QuizEngine.js at _app/components/QuizEngine.js (33KB shared engine). WSA engine at _app/houses/cloud/modules/wsa/quiz-engine.js (12KB). 157 standalone quizzes across _app/houses/{cloud,forge,eye,shield,script,web,key}/quizzes/*.quiz.html.

3. NEURAL PATHWAY (horizontal) — synaptic corridors with electrical arcs, tentacle enemies. Boss: Synapse Overload (brain-like structure with multiple attack nodes).
4. ENCRYPTION CHAMBER (vertical) — crystalline encrypted data structures, maze-like passages. Boss: Cipher Core (rotating encrypted sphere, decode weak points).
5. ROOTKIT DEPTHS (horizontal) — deep system layer, organic walls morphing, stealth enemies that appear suddenly. Boss: Kernel Parasite (worm-like creature threading through walls).
6. ZELOS CORE (horizontal) — final stage inside the malware entity itself, all enemy types return, environmental hazards. Boss: Zelos Protocol (multi-phase final boss — mouth → tentacles → core).

ENEMY TYPES:
- Drone Cells — basic enemies, straight-line movement
- Antibody Swarm — sine-wave pattern, comes in groups of 5
- Turret Nodes — embedded in walls, fire at angles
- Spore Launchers — stationary, release homing projectiles
- Data Worms — snake-like multi-segment enemies
- Stealth Fragments — appear suddenly from background
- Shield Carriers — frontal shield, must hit from behind
- Carrier Ships — large enemies that release smaller drones when destroyed

TECH IMPLEMENTATION:
- Canvas 2D, 60fps, tile-based scrolling
- Horizontal: background scrolls left-to-right at constant speed
- Vertical: background scrolls bottom-to-top at constant speed
- Parallax layers: 3 background layers at different scroll speeds
- Procedural organic/circuit textures for walls and backgrounds

- Web Audio API for chiptune BGM + laser/explosion SFX
- Integration: GameTracker.record('lifeforce', {...}), AchievementManager, GameScoreboard
- Single HTML file, shield house game

SCOPE MVP: 2 stages (1 horizontal + 1 vertical), powerup bar, 4 enemy types, 2 bosses. Expand to 6 stages if successful.

sprints.title: IDE Sequence — Terminal mastery & shell integration

sprints.title: IDE Sequence — Debugging, IntelliSense & productivity

DEBUGGING: launch.json anatomy, launch vs attach, breakpoints (line, conditional, logpoints), stepping (over, into, out, continue), Watch panel, Call Stack, Variables panel, Debug Console (evaluate expressions live), compound launch configs (debug frontend + backend simultaneously). INTELLISENSE: autocomplete, parameter hints, hover info, go to definition (F12), peek definition (Alt+F12), go to references, rename symbol (F2), code actions (lightbulb). PRODUCTIVITY: multi-cursor (Alt+Click, Ctrl+D for next match, Ctrl+Shift+L for all matches), find & replace with regex, Emmet abbreviations (HTML/CSS), bracket pair colorization, minimap, breadcrumbs navigation, sticky scroll, code folding, linked editing (rename HTML tags). REFACTORING: extract function/variable, move to new file, organize imports. Hands-on: debug a real script step by step.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Concepts & first repo (init, add, commit, status)
sprints.notes: Module 1 of Git deep dive. Visual commit graph showing how commits chain together. Working directory → staging area → repository diagram. Both terminal commands AND VS Code Source Control panel side by side. Interactive commit graph visualization that builds as student works.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Branching & merging (visual branch diagrams)
sprints.notes: Module 2. THE key module — branches MUST be visual. Animated branch/merge diagrams showing: create branch, diverging commits, fast-forward merge, 3-way merge. Show branch pointer movement. Terminal (git branch, checkout, switch, merge) + VS Code branch picker. Interactive: student creates branches and sees the graph update in real-time.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Merge conflicts & resolution
sprints.notes: Module 3. Visual diff view showing conflict markers (<<<< ==== >>>>). Walk through conflict resolution step by step. Show VS Code merge editor (inline accept/reject buttons, 3-way merge view). Terminal resolution workflow (edit, add, commit). Lab: deliberately create conflicts and resolve them.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Remotes, repos, forks & upstream
sprints.notes: Module 4. No detail spared. REPOS: what a repository actually is (the .git directory, object database, refs), bare vs non-bare repos, repo hosting (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket), creating repos (init vs clone), repo visibility (public/private), README/LICENSE/.gitignore conventions, repo settings & branch protection rules. FORKS: what a fork is vs a clone (visual diagram showing fork = server-side copy, clone = local copy), why fork (contributing to projects you dont own), the fork → clone → branch → PR → upstream merge cycle, keeping your fork in sync (add upstream remote, fetch upstream, merge/rebase), visual showing origin (your fork) vs upstream (original repo). REMOTES: git remote add/remove/rename, origin vs upstream naming convention, fetch vs pull (diagram), push with -u, tracking branches (origin/main vs main), multiple remotes for different workflows. VS Code: clone from GitHub, publish to GitHub, sync button behavior, GitHub Pull Requests extension.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Rebase, cherry-pick & history rewriting
sprints.notes: Module 5. Advanced but essential. Visual comparison: merge vs rebase (before/after branch diagrams). Interactive rebase (squash, reword, reorder). Cherry-pick with visual commit selection. Amend commits. Reflog as safety net. When to rebase vs merge decision guide.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Git workflows (Gitflow, trunk-based, GitHub flow)
sprints.notes: Module 6. Visual workflow diagrams for each strategy: Gitflow (develop/feature/release/hotfix branches), GitHub Flow (main + feature branches + PRs), trunk-based (short-lived branches, feature flags). Pros/cons comparison table. Which workflow for which team size/project type.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Tags, stash, blame, bisect & advanced tools
sprints.notes: Module 7. Utility commands: tags (lightweight vs annotated, semver), stash (save/pop/list/drop), blame (who changed what), bisect (binary search for bugs), log formatting (--oneline, --graph, --all). VS Code: GitLens extension, timeline view, blame annotations.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Git in VS Code (Source Control deep dive)

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — What are containers & why they exist
sprints.notes: Module 1 of Docker deep dive. Start from WHY — the "works on my machine" problem. VIRTUAL MACHINES VS CONTAINERS: visual comparison diagram (full OS stack vs shared kernel), hypervisor vs container runtime, resource overhead comparison. DOCKER ARCHITECTURE: Docker Engine (daemon, CLI, REST API), containerd, runc. Visual: client-server architecture diagram. CORE CONCEPTS: images (blueprints, read-only), containers (running instances, writable layer), registries (Docker Hub = app store for images). THE CONTAINER LIFECYCLE: visual state diagram — created → running → paused → stopped → removed. FIRST CONTAINER: docker run hello-world (what actually happens — pull → create → start → output → exit), docker run -it ubuntu bash (interactive container), docker run -d nginx (detached mode). BASIC COMMANDS: docker ps (running), docker ps -a (all), docker stop, docker start, docker rm, docker images, docker rmi. Visual: layered filesystem diagram showing image layers stacked, container writable layer on top. Every concept gets a diagram before the command.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Docker Compose & multi-container apps
sprints.notes: Module 5. Single containers are easy — real apps need multiple services. WHY COMPOSE: managing multiple docker run commands is painful, compose defines everything in one YAML file. COMPOSE FILE ANATOMY: version, services, networks, volumes — line by line walkthrough. Visual: multi-service architecture diagram (web → api → db → cache) with ports and networks labeled. SERVICES: image vs build, ports, environment, depends_on, restart policies, command/entrypoint override. VOLUMES IN COMPOSE: named volumes, bind mounts, tmpfs, volume drivers. Visual: data persistence diagram (container dies, volume survives). NETWORKING IN COMPOSE: default network (all services can reach each other by service name), custom networks, isolating frontend from backend. COMMANDS: docker compose up -d, docker compose down, docker compose logs -f, docker compose exec, docker compose ps, docker compose build --no-cache, docker compose pull. PROFILES: docker compose --profile debug up (conditional services). ENVIRONMENT: .env file with compose, variable substitution, multiple env files. LAB: build a 3-service app from scratch — Node/Python web app + PostgreSQL + Redis. docker-compose.yml with health checks, named volumes, custom network.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Pods, ReplicaSets & Deployments
sprints.notes: Module 2 of K8s deep dive. PODS: smallest deployable unit, one or more containers sharing network/storage, pod lifecycle (Pending → Running → Succeeded/Failed), pod YAML anatomy (apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec, containers), running a pod (kubectl run, kubectl apply -f). Visual: pod diagram showing containers + shared localhost + shared volumes inside the pod boundary. REPLICASETS: why you never run bare pods in production — ReplicaSet ensures N copies are always running, self-healing (kill a pod → new one spawns), selector + template pattern. Visual: ReplicaSet maintaining 3 pods, one dies, replacement created. DEPLOYMENTS: the object you actually use (manages ReplicaSets for you), deployment YAML walkthrough (replicas, selector, template, strategy), create/apply/delete. Visual: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods hierarchy diagram. LABELS & SELECTORS: how K8s connects objects (Deployment finds its pods via label selectors), matchLabels, label conventions (app, version, environment, team). kubectl get pods --show-labels, kubectl get pods -l app=nginx.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — ConfigMaps, Secrets & environment config
sprints.notes: Module 5. Separating config from code — the twelve-factor app way. CONFIGMAPS: what they are (key-value store for non-sensitive config), creating from literal (--from-literal), from file (--from-file), from env file (--from-env-file), from YAML manifest. Consuming: as environment variables (envFrom, valueFrom), as mounted volume files (config files appear in container filesystem). Visual: ConfigMap → Pod injection diagram. SECRETS: like ConfigMaps but base64 encoded (NOT encrypted by default — important to teach), types (Opaque, docker-registry, tls), creating secrets, consuming as env vars or volume mounts, why you need external secret managers in production (Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, Vault). BEST PRACTICES: never hardcode config in images, use ConfigMaps for non-sensitive config, Secrets for credentials, immutable ConfigMaps/Secrets (recreate dont update), environment-specific overlays with Kustomize.

sprints.title: CI/CD Sequence — Pipeline concepts & GitHub Actions

Covers: workflow file anatomy (.github/workflows/), YAML syntax for workflows, trigger events (push, pull_request, schedule, workflow_dispatch, repository_dispatch), jobs & steps, runners (hosted vs self-hosted), expressions & contexts (github, env, secrets, needs), matrix strategies, concurrency control, job outputs & dependencies, composite actions, reusable workflows (workflow_call), caching (actions/cache, setup-node cache), artifacts (upload/download), timeout & retry. sprints.title: Git Sequence — Repository anatomy (what lives inside .git)
sprints.notes: Deep dive into what a repo actually IS. Walk through .git/ directory: objects (blobs, trees, commits, tags), refs (branches = pointers to commits), HEAD, index (staging area), hooks, config. Visual: object graph showing how commits reference trees reference blobs. Demystify the magic — students should understand that a branch is just a 40-char file pointing to a commit hash. Show git cat-file, git log --graph --oneline --all. This foundational understanding makes everything else click.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Forks, upstream & open-source contribution workflow
sprints.notes: Full open-source contribution cycle, no steps skipped. Visual: fork diagram showing original repo → your fork (GitHub server-side copy) → your local clone (3 copies of the code). Step by step: (1) Fork on GitHub, (2) clone YOUR fork locally, (3) add upstream remote pointing to original, (4) create feature branch, (5) make changes + commit, (6) push to YOUR fork (origin), (7) open PR from your fork to upstream, (8) respond to review, (9) PR merged by maintainer, (10) sync your fork (fetch upstream, merge upstream/main, push to origin). Visual showing origin vs upstream at every step. Cover: why forks exist (permission model — you cant push to repos you dont own), fork vs branch (when to use which), keeping fork updated (stale fork problems), deleting fork branches after PR merge. GitHub-specific: fork button, comparing across forks, syncing fork via GitHub UI.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — GitHub features (Issues, PRs, Actions, Projects, Releases)
sprints.notes: GitHub is the DevOps engineers platform. Cover the full feature set: Issues (templates, labels, milestones, assignees), Pull Requests (draft PRs, reviewers, checks, merge strategies — merge/squash/rebase, auto-merge), GitHub Actions (workflow triggers, status checks on PRs), Projects (kanban boards, automation), Releases (tags → releases, changelogs, assets), branch protection rules (require reviews, require status checks, restrict force push), CODEOWNERS file, GitHub Pages. Visual: PR lifecycle diagram from branch creation to merged and deployed.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — .gitignore, README, LICENSE & repo conventions
sprints.notes: The files that make a repo professional. .gitignore: syntax (globs, negation, comments), global gitignore, gitignore.io, common patterns (node_modules, __pycache__, .env, build/). README.md: anatomy of a good README (title, badges, description, install, usage, contributing, license), markdown formatting. LICENSE: MIT, Apache 2.0, GPL — when to use which, choosealicense.com. CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md, CHANGELOG.md, .editorconfig, .prettierrc. These are the conventions a DevOps engineer enforces across all repos.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Diff & comparing changes
sprints.notes: Module: The diff command in full detail. Visual: 3-zone diagram (working directory → staging area → repository) showing where each diff command looks. git diff (working vs staged), git diff --staged (staged vs last commit), git diff HEAD (working vs last commit), git diff branch1..branch2 (compare branches), git diff commit1 commit2 (compare commits), git diff --stat (summary view), git diff -- filename (single file). Reading diff output: --- a/ +++ b/, @@ hunk headers, context lines, additions (green +), deletions (red -). VS Code: inline diff view, gutter indicators (green bar = added, blue = modified, red triangle = deleted), diff editor (side-by-side vs inline toggle), comparing branches in Source Control. Practical: diffing before committing is a daily habit — always review what you are about to commit.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Undoing things (reset, revert, restore, clean)
sprints.notes: Module: Every way to undo in Git, when to use which. Visual decision tree: "Did you push it?" → yes = revert, no = reset. RESET: git reset --soft HEAD~1 (undo commit, keep staged), git reset --mixed HEAD~1 (undo commit, unstage, keep working — the default), git reset --hard HEAD~1 (nuclear — lose everything). Visual: 3 diagrams showing what each mode preserves vs destroys. Reset to unstage: git reset HEAD file (or git restore --staged file). REVERT: git revert <commit> (creates a NEW commit that undoes a previous one — safe for shared history). Revert a merge commit (revert -m 1). RESTORE: git restore file (discard working dir changes), git restore --staged file (unstage), git restore --source=HEAD~2 file (restore from specific commit). CLEAN: git clean -n (dry run), git clean -fd (remove untracked files and dirs). REFLOG as safety net: git reflog shows everything, even after reset --hard. Recovering "lost" commits with reflog + checkout/branch. Amend: git commit --amend (rewrite last commit message or add forgotten files — only before push). VS Code: discard changes, unstage, timeline to restore old versions. WARNING BOX: never reset --hard or amend on commits you have already pushed.

sprints.title: Git Sequence — Tips, tricks & dark arts
sprints.notes: The module that makes students dangerous. ALIASES: git config --global alias.co checkout, alias.br branch, alias.st status, alias.lg for pretty log graph, alias.undo for reset HEAD~1. SHORTCUTS: git commit -am (add+commit tracked files), git push --force-with-lease (safe force push), git switch - (previous branch like cd -), git stash pop vs apply, git log -p -S"searchterm" (pickaxe — find when a string was added/removed), git shortlog -sn (contributor leaderboard). POWER MOVES: git worktrees (multiple branches checked out simultaneously), git rerere (reuse recorded resolution — auto-resolve repeated conflicts), git filter-branch / git-filter-repo (rewrite history to remove secrets/large files), git sparse-checkout (partial clone for monorepos), git submodules vs subtrees (embedding repos inside repos), git hooks (pre-commit, pre-push, commit-msg — automate quality checks). DEBUGGING: git log --all --graph --oneline --decorate (the god log), git reflog for time travel, git fsck for repo integrity, git gc and object packing, git blame -L 10,20 file (blame specific lines), git log --follow file (track renames). .GITCONFIG TRICKS: conditional includes ([includeIf] for work vs personal email), credential helpers, diff.tool and merge.tool config, core.autocrlf for cross-platform teams. FORMAT: Fun, fast-paced, "did you know?" energy. Each tip gets a before/after showing the slow way vs the shortcut.

sprints.title: IDE Sequence — File management, explorer & project structure
sprints.notes: Module: How files and projects actually work in VS Code. EXPLORER PANEL: file tree navigation, create/rename/delete/move files and folders, drag & drop, collapse all, filter files in explorer, sort by name/type/modified. OPENING PROJECTS: File > Open Folder (THIS is how you open projects — not individual files), recent folders, workspaces. MULTI-ROOT WORKSPACES: .code-workspace files, adding multiple folders to one workspace, per-folder settings, when to use (monorepos, related projects). FILE OPERATIONS: new file (Ctrl+N), save/save as/save all, auto-save settings (afterDelay, onFocusChange, onWindowChange), hot exit (unsaved files survive restart). TABS & EDITORS: tab management, pin tabs, split editors (vertical/horizontal), editor groups, preview mode (single click = preview, double click = keep open), side-by-side compare. PROJECT STRUCTURE CONVENTIONS: where things go in a typical project (src/, tests/, docs/, config/, .github/), recognizing project types by their files (package.json = Node, requirements.txt = Python, Cargo.toml = Rust, pom.xml = Java). sprints.notes: Module: Understanding file extensions and how VS Code handles them. LANGUAGE EXTENSIONS: installing language packs (Python, Go, Rust, Java, C++), what they provide (IntelliSense, linting, formatting, debugging). FORMATTERS & LINTERS: Prettier, ESLint, Black, autopep8 — format on save, format on paste, default formatter setting. ENCODING: UTF-8 vs others, BOM, line endings (LF vs CRLF — critical for cross-platform teams), .editorconfig for team consistency. sprints.title: IDE Sequence — Remote development (SSH, WSL, containers, tunnels)
sprints.notes: Module: DevOps engineers work on remote machines constantly. This is essential. REMOTE - SSH: install Remote-SSH extension, configure ~/.ssh/config hosts, connect to remote server, VS Code runs on remote (full IntelliSense, terminal, debugging on the server), port forwarding (access remote port locally), transfer files. REMOTE - WSL: open WSL distro, install in WSL, seamless Linux dev on Windows, file system performance (always work in WSL filesystem not /mnt/c). REMOTE - CONTAINERS (Dev Containers): .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, open folder in container, Dockerfile-based dev environment, features, port forwarding, volume mounts, "everyone gets the same environment". REMOTE - TUNNELS: code tunnel (expose local VS Code to browser), GitHub Codespaces (cloud-hosted dev environment), when to use which remote method. SSH DEEP DIVE: key-based auth, ProxyJump for bastion hosts, agent forwarding, multiplexing (ControlMaster), SSH config file patterns for managing dozens of servers. PRACTICAL: connect to a remote server, edit files, run commands, forward a port, debug remotely — all without leaving VS Code.

sprints.title: IDE Sequence — Essential DevOps extensions toolkit
sprints.notes: Module: The extensions that make VS Code a DevOps powerhouse. Curated toolkit, not a list dump — each extension gets a WHY and a demo. GIT: GitLens (blame, graph, file history, compare branches), Git Graph (visual commit graph). CONTAINERS: Docker extension (build/run/manage images and containers, Dockerfile IntelliSense, compose support), Kubernetes extension (cluster explorer, manifest IntelliSense, apply/delete resources). CI/CD: GitHub Actions (workflow syntax highlighting, validation, run status), YAML (Red Hat — schema validation for K8s, Docker Compose, GitHub Actions, Ansible). IAC: HashiCorp Terraform (HCL syntax, IntelliSense, format on save, terraform plan integration), AWS Toolkit, Azure Tools. API TESTING: REST Client (send HTTP requests from .http files — replaces Postman for quick tests), Thunder Client (full GUI API client inside VS Code). REMOTE: Remote - SSH, Remote - WSL, Dev Containers (covered in DO-45 but listed here for the toolkit). LANGUAGES: Python, Pylance, ESLint, Prettier. UTILITIES: Path Intellisense (autocomplete file paths), Error Lens (inline error display), TODO Highlight, Markdown Preview Enhanced, indent-rainbow, Better Comments. FORMAT: each extension shown with screenshot/demo of what it does, install command, key settings to configure.

sprints.title: IDE Sequence — VS Code tips, shortcuts & power user secrets
sprints.notes: The module that turns beginners into power users. NAVIGATION SHORTCUTS: Ctrl+P (quick open file — type partial name), Ctrl+Shift+P (command palette), Ctrl+G (go to line), Ctrl+Shift+O (go to symbol in file), Ctrl+T (go to symbol in workspace), Ctrl+Tab (switch tabs), Ctrl+ (split editor), Ctrl+B (toggle sidebar), Ctrl+J (toggle panel), Ctrl+K Ctrl+S (keyboard shortcuts viewer). EDITING SHORTCUTS: Ctrl+D (select next occurrence), Ctrl+Shift+L (select ALL occurrences), Alt+Up/Down (move line), Shift+Alt+Up/Down (duplicate line), Ctrl+Shift+K (delete line), Ctrl+/ (toggle comment), Ctrl+[ / ] (indent/outdent), Ctrl+Shift+[ / ] (fold/unfold). MULTI-CURSOR MASTERY: Alt+Click, Ctrl+Alt+Up/Down (add cursor above/below), box selection (Shift+Alt+drag), find and add cursors to all matches. ZEN MODE: Ctrl+K Z (distraction-free), toggle minimap, toggle breadcrumbs, toggle activity bar. POWER TRICKS: settings.json hacks ("editor.wordWrap", "editor.formatOnSave", "editor.bracketPairColorization.enabled", "workbench.editor.enablePreview": false), workspace-specific settings vs global, command line: code . (open folder), code -r . (reuse window), code --diff file1 file2 (diff from terminal). SNIPPETS: built-in snippets, creating custom snippets (prefix, body, tabstops, variables), project-specific snippets in .vscode/. FORMAT: fast-paced, tip cards with keyboard shortcut displayed prominently, before/after showing the slow way vs the fast way.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Dockerfile deep dive (writing, building, optimizing)
sprints.notes: Module 2. The Dockerfile is the DevOps engineers recipe. INSTRUCTIONS LINE BY LINE: FROM (base image selection — alpine vs slim vs full, why it matters), RUN (executing commands, chaining with &&, cleaning up apt cache), COPY vs ADD (COPY is preferred, ADD for URLs/tar extraction), WORKDIR (set working directory, avoid cd), ENV (environment variables), EXPOSE (documentation, does NOT publish ports), CMD vs ENTRYPOINT (exec form vs shell form, when to use which, how they combine), ARG (build-time variables), USER (non-root!), LABEL (metadata), HEALTHCHECK (container self-diagnostics). BUILD CONTEXT: what gets sent to daemon, .dockerignore (critical — like .gitignore for Docker, prevent sending node_modules/secrets/.git). LAYER CACHING: how Docker caches layers, order matters (copy package.json before source code), cache busting. MULTI-STAGE BUILDS: visual showing build stage → production stage, compile in one image, copy binary to tiny final image, dramatic size reduction (1.2GB → 80MB example). IMAGE SIZE OPTIMIZATION: minimal base images, combining RUN commands, removing unnecessary files, using --no-install-recommends. BEST PRACTICES: one process per container, use specific image tags (not :latest in production), lint with hadolint. Visual: layer diagram showing each instruction creating a new layer.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Docker CLI mastery (exec, logs, inspect, debug)
sprints.notes: Module 3. The commands you use every single day. INSPECTING CONTAINERS: docker inspect (JSON output — IP address, mounts, env vars, state), docker logs (stdout/stderr, --follow, --tail, --since, timestamps), docker stats (live CPU/memory/network/IO — like top for containers), docker top (processes inside container), docker port (port mappings), docker diff (filesystem changes since start). INTERACTING: docker exec -it container bash (shell into running container — the most used debug command), docker exec container command (run a command without shell), docker cp (copy files in/out of container), docker attach (attach to main process — careful, Ctrl+C kills it). LIFECYCLE: docker create vs run, docker pause/unpause, docker rename, docker wait (block until container exits), docker restart. CLEANUP: docker rm (remove stopped containers), docker container prune (remove ALL stopped), docker image prune (dangling images), docker volume prune (unused volumes), docker system prune -a (nuclear cleanup — reclaim disk space), docker system df (show disk usage). RESOURCE LIMITS: docker run --memory=512m --cpus=1.5 (prevent container from eating the host). FORMATTING OUTPUT: docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}	{{.Status}}	{{.Ports}}" (custom output), --filter for targeted queries. Each command shown with real output examples.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Images, registries & tagging strategy
sprints.notes: Module 4. DevOps engineers manage images across environments. IMAGES DEEP DIVE: docker images (list), docker image inspect (layers, size, config), docker history (see every layer and its size), image IDs vs tags (an image can have multiple tags, tags are just pointers). TAGGING: docker tag (create new tag for existing image), tagging strategy — semver (v1.2.3), latest (what it actually means — just a convention, NOT automatically the newest), environment tags (dev, staging, prod), git SHA tags (immutable, traceable to exact commit). Visual: diagram showing one image with multiple tags pointing to same digest. REGISTRIES: Docker Hub (public, official images, verified publishers, rate limits), GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io — tied to repos), AWS ECR, Azure ACR, Google GCR, self-hosted (Harbor). PUSH/PULL: docker login, docker push (requires registry/repo:tag format), docker pull (explicit vs implicit in docker run), docker manifest inspect (multi-arch images). PRIVATE REGISTRIES: authentication, credential helpers, .docker/config.json. IMAGE SCANNING: docker scout (built-in vulnerability scanning), Trivy, Snyk, scanning in CI pipelines (block deployment on critical CVEs). CLEANUP: removing old images, automated cleanup policies in registries. Best practice: never deploy :latest to production, always pin specific tags.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Networking (bridge, host, DNS, port mapping)
sprints.notes: Module 6. Containers need to talk to each other and the outside world. NETWORK DRIVERS: bridge (default — isolated network per host, containers communicate via IP/DNS), host (container shares host network stack — no isolation, full speed), none (no networking — maximum isolation), overlay (multi-host networking for Swarm/distributed systems), macvlan (container gets own MAC address on physical network). Visual: diagram for each driver showing container ↔ host ↔ external traffic flow. DEFAULT BRIDGE: docker0 interface, containers get IPs from subnet, port publishing (-p host:container), why containers on default bridge cant resolve each other by name. USER-DEFINED BRIDGE: docker network create, automatic DNS resolution (container name = hostname), isolating groups of containers, connecting container to multiple networks. PORT MAPPING: -p 8080:80 (host:container), -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 (bind to specific interface), -P (publish all exposed ports to random host ports), EXPOSE in Dockerfile vs -p at runtime. DNS: Docker embedded DNS server (127.0.0.11), container name resolution, --dns flag, /etc/resolv.conf inside containers. DEBUGGING NETWORK ISSUES: docker network inspect, docker exec ping/curl, docker logs for connection errors, nsenter for advanced debugging. Lab: create isolated networks, connect services, test cross-network communication.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Volumes & persistent data
sprints.notes: Module 7. Containers are ephemeral — data must survive. THE PROBLEM: visual showing container removed → data gone. Everything inside the writable layer dies with the container. THREE STORAGE TYPES: volumes (Docker-managed, stored in /var/lib/docker/volumes/, best for persistent data), bind mounts (map host directory into container, best for development — live code editing), tmpfs mounts (in-memory only, never written to disk, best for secrets/sensitive data during build). Visual: diagram comparing all three showing where data lives on host. VOLUMES: docker volume create, docker volume ls, docker volume inspect (shows mountpoint), docker volume rm, docker volume prune. Using volumes: docker run -v myvolume:/app/data (named volume), -v /app/data (anonymous volume). BIND MOUNTS: docker run -v /host/path:/container/path, read-only mounts (:ro), hot reloading for development (mount source code, changes reflect instantly). BACKUP & RESTORE: docker run --volumes-from to mount another containers volumes, backup volume to tar (docker run -v myvolume:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/backup.tar.gz /data). VOLUME DRIVERS: local (default), NFS, cloud storage plugins. PERMISSIONS: UID/GID issues between host and container, --user flag, chown in Dockerfile. BEST PRACTICES: never store data in container layer, use named volumes over anonymous, separate data volumes from code volumes, backup strategy.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Security & production best practices
sprints.notes: Module 8. Running Docker in production requires security hardening. NON-ROOT: why running as root inside containers is dangerous (container escape → host root), USER instruction in Dockerfile, --user flag at runtime, rootless Docker mode. IMAGE SECURITY: use official/verified base images, pin specific versions (not :latest), scan for CVEs (docker scout, Trivy), minimal base images (distroless, scratch, alpine), dont install unnecessary packages. SECRETS: never bake secrets into images (they persist in layers!), docker secret (Swarm), --mount type=secret in BuildKit, environment variables (visible in docker inspect — use cautiously), secret management (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager). RESOURCE LIMITS: --memory, --cpus, --pids-limit, OOM killer behavior, ulimits. READ-ONLY: --read-only flag (immutable filesystem), --tmpfs for writable temp dirs. CAPABILITIES: drop all capabilities --cap-drop=ALL, add back only what is needed --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE, no-new-privileges flag. NETWORKING: dont use --network=host in production, limit published ports, use internal networks for backend services. LOGGING: logging drivers (json-file, syslog, fluentd), log rotation (--log-opt max-size=10m max-file=3), centralized logging architecture. HEALTH CHECKS: HEALTHCHECK instruction, --health-cmd, --health-interval, container orchestrator uses these for restart decisions. DOCKER DAEMON SECURITY: TLS for remote API, restricting who can access the Docker socket. Checklist format: production readiness checklist students can reference.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Real-world patterns & architecture
sprints.notes: Module 9. How Docker is used in actual production environments. PATTERNS: sidecar containers (logging, monitoring agents alongside main app), init containers (run setup before main container starts), ambassador pattern (proxy for external services), adapter pattern (normalize interfaces). MULTI-ENVIRONMENT: same image, different config — dev/staging/prod via environment variables, config files mounted as volumes, feature flags. CI/CD WITH DOCKER: build image in CI → push to registry → deploy to staging → promote to production, Docker layer caching in CI (speed up builds), docker buildx for multi-architecture images (amd64 + arm64). DEBUGGING CRASHED CONTAINERS: docker logs on exited container, docker cp to extract files, docker commit (snapshot container state to new image for inspection), docker events (real-time event stream). MONITORING: docker stats, cAdvisor, Prometheus + Grafana for container metrics. ORCHESTRATION PREVIEW: why single-host Docker is not enough for production — leads into Kubernetes sequence. Visual: real-world architecture diagram showing load balancer → multiple container instances → database → cache → message queue, with volumes and networks labeled.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Hands-on lab (build, ship, run)
sprints.notes: Comprehensive hands-on lab. Challenge sequence: (1) Write a Dockerfile for a Python/Node web app from scratch (multi-stage build, non-root user, health check), (2) Build and tag the image with semver, (3) Run container with port mapping and environment variables, (4) Create a docker-compose.yml adding database and cache services, (5) Add named volumes for database persistence, (6) Create custom network isolating frontend from database, (7) Exec into running container to debug, (8) View logs and stats, (9) Stop, prune, clean up. Simulated environment with validation at each step. Both terminal commands and VS Code Docker extension workflows shown.

sprints.title: Docker Sequence — Tips, tricks & shortcuts
sprints.notes: The Docker power user module. ALIASES: alias d=docker, alias dc="docker compose", alias dps="docker ps --format table", alias dclean="docker system prune -af". SHELL TRICKS: docker exec into container with custom shell (bash || sh fallback), copy output from container to clipboard, pipe output between containers, run one-off commands (docker run --rm -it alpine sh). BUILDKIT: DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 (faster builds, better caching, secrets mounting, SSH forwarding during build), buildx for multi-platform builds. SPEED: .dockerignore reduces build context (seconds vs minutes), layer ordering for cache hits, using --target for partial multi-stage builds, parallel stage execution. COMPOSE TRICKS: docker compose up --build (rebuild on every up), docker compose run --rm service command (one-off without starting everything), extends and anchors in YAML (&anchor *alias), override files (docker-compose.override.yml auto-loaded in dev). DEBUGGING: docker run --entrypoint sh image (override entrypoint to get shell), docker history --no-trunc (see full commands in layers), docker inspect --format (Go templates for specific fields), dive tool (explore image layers interactively). VS CODE: Docker extension — right-click to run/stop/remove/logs/exec, Dockerfile IntelliSense, compose graph visualization. Before/after format: the slow way vs the trick.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Why Kubernetes & architecture overview
sprints.notes: Module 1. Start from the problem Docker alone cant solve. THE PROBLEM: you have 50 containers across 10 servers — who decides where they run? What happens when a server dies? How do you update without downtime? How do you scale? Manual docker run on each server doesnt work. WHAT K8S IS: container orchestration platform — automates deployment, scaling, and management. Not a replacement for Docker — it USES Docker (or containerd). Visual: before K8s (manual chaos) vs after K8s (orchestrated order). ARCHITECTURE: Control Plane (API Server — the front door, etcd — the database, Scheduler — where to place pods, Controller Manager — desired state loops) + Worker Nodes (kubelet — node agent, kube-proxy — networking, container runtime). Visual: full architecture diagram with arrows showing communication flow. API-driven: everything is a REST API call, kubectl is just an API client. DESIRED STATE MODEL: you declare WHAT you want (3 replicas of nginx), K8s figures out HOW to make it happen and KEEPS it that way. Reconciliation loop concept. OBJECTS: everything is a resource/object (Pod, Service, Deployment, etc.), YAML manifests describe desired state, kubectl apply sends to API server. DISTRIBUTIONS: managed K8s (EKS, AKS, GKE) vs self-hosted vs local dev (minikube, kind, k3d). For learning: minikube or kind.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — kubectl mastery (the daily driver CLI)
sprints.notes: Module 3. kubectl is to K8s what git is to version control — you use it all day every day. BASICS: kubectl get (pods, services, deployments, nodes, all), kubectl describe (detailed info + events — your first debug tool), kubectl logs (container stdout/stderr, --follow, --previous for crashed pods, --container for multi-container pods), kubectl exec -it pod -- bash (shell into pod), kubectl delete, kubectl apply -f vs kubectl create. OUTPUT FORMATTING: -o wide (extra columns), -o yaml (full YAML), -o json (for scripting), -o jsonpath (extract specific fields), -o custom-columns (build your own table), --sort-by. CONTEXT & NAMESPACE: kubectl config get-contexts (which cluster am I talking to?), kubectl config use-context, kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=prod, kubectx/kubens tools for fast switching. DRY RUN: kubectl apply --dry-run=client -o yaml (generate YAML without applying — great for learning). LABELS: kubectl get pods -l app=web, kubectl label pod mypod env=prod, kubectl get all --selector=team=backend. EXPLAIN: kubectl explain pod.spec.containers (built-in API docs — shows every field and what it means). ALIASES: alias k=kubectl, kubectl completion bash (tab completion — essential). IMPERATIVE VS DECLARATIVE: kubectl create (imperative — one-time) vs kubectl apply (declarative — idempotent, what you use in production). Quick reference card format with the 20 commands you use 80% of the time.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Services & networking (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, Ingress)
sprints.notes: Module 4. Pods get random IPs that change — Services provide stable networking. WHY SERVICES: pods are ephemeral (IP changes on restart), Service gives a stable IP + DNS name, load balances across matching pods. Visual: 3 pods behind a Service, request flows to any healthy pod. SERVICE TYPES: ClusterIP (default — internal only, other pods can reach it, used for backend APIs and databases), NodePort (exposes on every nodes IP at a static port 30000-32767, used for dev/testing), LoadBalancer (provisions cloud load balancer, used in production on EKS/AKS/GKE, gets external IP), ExternalName (DNS alias to external service). Visual: side-by-side diagrams of each type showing traffic flow from client to pod. SERVICE YAML: spec.selector (matches pod labels), spec.ports (port vs targetPort vs nodePort), spec.type. KUBE-DNS: every Service gets a DNS entry (service-name.namespace.svc.cluster.local), short names work within same namespace. INGRESS: why you dont want 50 LoadBalancers (expensive), Ingress = single entry point with path-based routing, Ingress Controller (nginx-ingress, traefik, ALB Ingress), Ingress YAML (rules, hosts, paths, TLS), visual showing domain → Ingress → multiple Services. NETWORK POLICIES: restrict pod-to-pod traffic (default = everything can talk to everything), allow/deny rules based on labels and namespaces, visual showing allowed vs blocked traffic paths. DEBUGGING: kubectl get endpoints (what IPs does the Service route to?), kubectl port-forward (access a Service from localhost without exposing), testing with curl from inside a pod.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Scaling, rolling updates & rollbacks
sprints.notes: Module 6. Scaling and zero-downtime deployments. MANUAL SCALING: kubectl scale deployment myapp --replicas=5, scaling to zero (save resources, pause service). HORIZONTAL POD AUTOSCALER (HPA): auto-scale based on CPU/memory, kubectl autoscale deployment myapp --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70, HPA YAML manifest, metrics server requirement, custom metrics (requests per second, queue depth). Visual: graph showing pod count adjusting to load over time. ROLLING UPDATES: the default strategy — Deployment updates pods gradually (new version pods come up while old ones terminate), strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge (how many extra pods during update), maxUnavailable (how many can be down), visual: step-by-step diagram showing old pods replaced by new pods with zero downtime. kubectl rollout status (watch the update), kubectl rollout history (see revision history). ROLLBACK: kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp (instant rollback to previous version), kubectl rollout undo --to-revision=3 (specific version), why rollback is fast (ReplicaSet for previous version still exists, just scales it back up). RECREATE STRATEGY: kill all old → start all new (has downtime, use for stateful apps that cant run two versions). CANARY DEPLOYMENTS: concept — route small % of traffic to new version, monitor, then full rollout. Blue/green deployments via Service selector swapping. Visual: canary showing 90% traffic to v1, 10% to v2.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Storage (PV, PVC, StorageClasses)
sprints.notes: Module 7. Persistent data in an ephemeral world. THE PROBLEM: pod dies → local data gone (same as Docker). K8s needs a way to decouple storage from pod lifecycle. VOLUMES: emptyDir (shared between containers in same pod, dies with pod), hostPath (mount host directory — avoid in production), projected volumes (combine configmaps/secrets/downwardAPI). PERSISTENT VOLUMES (PV): cluster-level storage resource, provisioned by admin, exists independently of pods. Visual: PV as a disk icon living outside any pod. PERSISTENT VOLUME CLAIMS (PVC): pod requests storage via PVC, K8s binds PVC to matching PV (like a storage voucher). Visual: Pod → PVC → PV → actual disk. Access modes: ReadWriteOnce (single node), ReadOnlyMany (multiple nodes read), ReadWriteMany (multiple nodes read-write — NFS/EFS). STORAGE CLASSES: dynamic provisioning — no admin needed, PVC requests a StorageClass and PV is auto-created, cloud providers (gp3 on AWS, pd-ssd on GCP, managed-premium on Azure). Reclaim policies: Retain (keep data), Delete (destroy with PVC). STATEFULSETS: when you need stable network identity + persistent storage per pod (databases, message queues), pod names are ordinal (mysql-0, mysql-1, mysql-2), volumeClaimTemplates. Visual: StatefulSet vs Deployment comparison diagram.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Namespaces, RBAC & multi-tenancy
sprints.notes: Module 8. Organizing and securing a shared cluster. NAMESPACES: virtual clusters within a cluster, default namespaces (default, kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease), creating namespaces, when to use (per team, per environment, per project), resource isolation. kubectl get pods -n production, kubectl get pods --all-namespaces. RESOURCE QUOTAS: limit CPU/memory/pod count per namespace, prevent one team from consuming entire cluster. LimitRange: default requests/limits for pods in namespace. RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): who can do what where. Subjects (Users, Groups, ServiceAccounts), Resources (pods, services, secrets), Verbs (get, list, create, delete, watch). Role + RoleBinding (namespace-scoped), ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-wide). YAML walkthrough for each. Visual: RBAC chain — User → RoleBinding → Role → allowed actions on resources. SERVICE ACCOUNTS: identity for pods (not humans), default ServiceAccount per namespace, pod uses ServiceAccount to authenticate to API server, least-privilege principle. SECURITY CONTEXTS: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, seccompProfile, pod-level vs container-level. Practical: set up namespace with quotas and RBAC so dev team can only access their own namespace.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Helm (package manager for Kubernetes)
sprints.notes: Module 9. Writing raw YAML for every app doesnt scale. WHY HELM: managing dozens of YAML files per app is painful, environment differences (dev vs prod) mean duplicated manifests, Helm solves this with templating and packaging. CONCEPTS: Charts (package of K8s manifests + templates), Releases (installed instance of a chart), Repositories (chart storage — like Docker Hub for Helm). CHART ANATOMY: Chart.yaml (metadata), values.yaml (defaults — the knobs users turn), templates/ directory (Go-templated K8s manifests), helpers.tpl (reusable template functions). Visual: values.yaml + template → rendered manifest. COMMANDS: helm repo add/update, helm search repo, helm install myrelease chart (deploy), helm upgrade (update), helm rollback (undo), helm uninstall (remove), helm list (see releases), helm status, helm history. VALUES: helm install -f myvalues.yaml (override defaults), --set key=value (inline override), values hierarchy (chart defaults → -f overrides → --set overrides). CREATING CHARTS: helm create mychart (scaffold), writing templates ({{ .Values.image.repository }}), conditionals ({{ if }}), loops ({{ range }}), named templates ({{ include }}). POPULAR CHARTS: nginx-ingress, cert-manager, prometheus, grafana — dont reinvent the wheel. HELMFILE: managing multiple charts across environments. Best practice: use Helm for third-party tools, consider Kustomize for your own apps.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Monitoring, logging & debugging
sprints.notes: Module 10. Things break — you need to find out why fast. DEBUGGING WORKFLOW: kubectl describe pod (check Events section first — scheduling failures, image pull errors, OOM kills), kubectl logs (application output, --previous for crashed pods), kubectl exec (shell in for live debugging), kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp. COMMON ISSUES AND FIXES: ImagePullBackOff (wrong image name, private registry auth), CrashLoopBackOff (app crashing — check logs, check command/args, check env vars), Pending (no node has enough resources, check kubectl describe node), OOMKilled (container exceeded memory limit — increase or fix leak), CreateContainerConfigError (missing ConfigMap or Secret). Visual: decision tree — pod not running? follow this flowchart. RESOURCE MONITORING: kubectl top pods/nodes (requires metrics-server), resource requests vs limits (requests = guaranteed minimum, limits = hard ceiling), QoS classes (Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort). OBSERVABILITY STACK: Prometheus (metrics collection, PromQL basics), Grafana (dashboards, pre-built K8s dashboards), Loki (log aggregation), alerting concepts. HEALTH PROBES: livenessProbe (is the container alive? restart if not), readinessProbe (is it ready for traffic? remove from Service if not), startupProbe (slow-starting containers). Probe types: httpGet, exec, tcpSocket, grpc. Visual: probe decision diagram — when each probe runs and what happens on failure.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Real-world patterns & production readiness
sprints.notes: Module 11. Production K8s patterns that real teams use. POD DESIGN PATTERNS: sidecar (logging/proxy containers alongside main app — Envoy, Fluentd), init containers (run setup tasks before app starts — migrations, config fetching, wait-for-db), ambassador (proxy to external service). RESOURCE MANAGEMENT: always set requests AND limits, right-sizing (start conservative, adjust based on metrics), Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) for automatic right-sizing. POD DISRUPTION BUDGETS: PDB ensures minimum availability during voluntary disruptions (node upgrades, scaling down), minAvailable or maxUnavailable. AFFINITY & ANTI-AFFINITY: control pod placement — spread across availability zones (podAntiAffinity), co-locate related pods (podAffinity), node affinity (run on GPU nodes). TAINTS & TOLERATIONS: reserve nodes for specific workloads, NoSchedule/PreferNoSchedule/NoExecute. JOBS & CRONJOBS: batch processing (Job runs to completion, parallelism, backoff limit), scheduled tasks (CronJob — K8s equivalent of cron, schedule syntax, concurrencyPolicy, successfulJobsHistoryLimit). KUSTOMIZE: template-free customization — base + overlays for environments, strategic merge patches, commonLabels/commonAnnotations. GITOPS: ArgoCD/Flux concepts — Git as single source of truth, auto-sync cluster state to repo, visual showing git push → ArgoCD detects → applies to cluster. PRODUCTION CHECKLIST: resource limits set, health probes configured, PDB defined, security context locked down, namespaces and RBAC configured, monitoring and alerting active, backup strategy for stateful workloads.

sprints.title: K8s Sequence — Tips, tricks & shortcuts

JSONPATH: kubectl get pods -o jsonpath="{.items[*].metadata.name}" (extract data for scripting), kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath="{.items[*].status.addresses[0].address}" (get all node IPs). sprints.title: Ansible Testing & CI Integration
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 11 — trust but verify. Covers: linting (ansible-lint — rules, profiles, custom rules, .ansible-lint config, yamllint integration), Molecule (test framework for roles — init, create, converge, idempotence, verify, destroy, drivers: Docker/Podman/Vagrant/cloud, verifiers: Ansible/testinfra/goss, test matrix for multiple platforms), check mode & diff mode (--check --diff, simulating changes, check_mode per task), assert module (validating state in playbooks), CI/CD integration (GitHub Actions + Molecule, GitLab CI + ansible-lint, Jenkins pipeline for Ansible), testing strategies (unit: molecule converge + verify, integration: full stack deploy + test, smoke: post-deployment health checks), playbook debugging (ansible-playbook -vvvv, debug module, debugger keyword, callback plugins — yaml, json, timer), performance testing (profiling with callback plugins, identifying slow tasks). Visual: Molecule test lifecycle diagram, CI pipeline for Ansible roles. Hands-on: add Molecule tests to a role, set up CI pipeline, debug a failing playbook.

sprints.title: Ansible Real-World Patterns & Lab
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 12 — putting it all together. Covers: real-world automation patterns — rolling updates (serial, max_fail_percentage, delegate_to for load balancer drain), blue/green deployments with Ansible, zero-downtime deployment playbooks, multi-tier application deployment (web + app + db, play-per-tier, delegation, run_once), compliance scanning (ansible-lint + custom rules, CIS benchmark playbooks), patch management (yum/apt update, reboot handling with wait_for_connection, maintenance windows), backup automation, monitoring agent deployment, user onboarding/offboarding. Project structure at scale (directory layout, environment separation, ansible.cfg per project, requirements.yml for dependencies). Anti-patterns: shell/command for everything, 1000-line playbooks, no error handling, running as root unnecessarily. Lab: deploy a full multi-tier application stack — provisioning, configuration, deployment, verification, rollback.

sprints.title: Ansible Tips, Tricks & Dark Arts
sprints.notes: Ansible track module 13 — hard-won wisdom. Covers: performance tuning (pipelining, ControlPersist, mitogen, forks, async + poll for long tasks, free strategy for independent hosts), callback plugins (yaml output, timer, profile_tasks — find slow tasks), custom modules (Python, write your own when built-ins don't fit), custom filters & plugins (filter_plugins/, lookup_plugins/, connection_plugins/), Ansible Navigator (next-gen CLI, TUI, EE integration), Execution Environments (containerized Ansible, ansible-builder, reproducible automation), ansible-pull (decentralized — nodes pull their own config from Git), event-driven Ansible (ansible-rulebook, Event-Driven Automation controller, webhook triggers), Ansible + Terraform integration patterns (Terraform provisions, Ansible configures, dynamic inventory bridge), migration tips (from shell scripts to Ansible, from Chef/Puppet to Ansible). Secret tricks: delegate_to localhost for API calls, throttle for rate-limited APIs, meta: clear_facts/clear_host_errors/end_play/end_host, ansible-inventory --graph --vars for debugging.
